Entertainment.title: Sally Rooney books including Normal People and Intermezzo withdrawn from sale in UK over author's Palestine Action support
Entertainment.text:
Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.

The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books to UK retailers.

"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.

Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.

Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.

Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.

Normal People was published in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.

Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.

Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."

Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."

Entertainment.title: 'People call them pervert glasses but they give me independence'
Entertainment.text:
Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.

A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.

For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information.

"I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says.

"If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace."

Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years.

They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public.

"People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online.

Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people.

"We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says.

"We're using them to lead an independent life."

Tracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns.

"I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says.

Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year.

It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities.

As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month.

This means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year.

He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked.

"Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip.

"I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group.

"You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses."

Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees.

The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices."

The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments.

Cosplay artist Spill The Tea was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed.

She later discovered the footage was posted online.

The performer, who has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated".

"He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist.

She says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities.

"For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says.

"They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them."

In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life.

"They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video.

"It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it."

Entertainment.title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
Entertainment.text:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.

Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.

"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.

"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."

The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after doctors had found a rare benign tumour, called a colloid cyst, in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.

In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.

She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.

Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [the hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.

"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."

A year ago, for the first time since the brain surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.

Entertainment.title: Danny Dyer sails River Thames with poo sculpture in water protest
Entertainment.text:
Actor Danny Dyer has delivered a petition to Downing Street calling for water companies to be nationalised after floating a giant poo sculpture down the River Thames on a boat.

Dyer and Sittingbourne and Sheppey MP Kevin McKenna sailed along the Thames with the sculpture as part of a protest calling for the water industry to be brought into public ownership.

The actor, who runs a caravan park on the Isle of Sheppey with daughter Dani Dyer, delivered the petition having previously joined a local sewage protest in Leysdown in September.

A government spokesperson said it would "give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible".

Nearly 350,000 people have signed the petition, started by campaigners SOS Whitstable.

Rivals actor Dyer and his daughter, who is currently competing on Strictly Come Dancing, joined the protest in September alongside singer Becky Hill, and Surfers Against Sewage.

He previously called the quality of bathing water "a disgrace", adding that issues with sewage discharges were "a very dangerous thing".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he wants to see "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors, but suggestions that water companies could be nationalised have received pushback, including from lenders to Thames Water.

A government spokesperson said the prime minister had been "clear that the failures of the past must be corrected".

It added: "We are bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

Entertainment.title: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween
Entertainment.text:
What could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing?

It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says host Jimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.”

Not that Last One Laughing is making serious moves into chiller territory: after all, why tamper with a format that’s given Prime Video such a huge hit? With over 2m people tuning in per episode, series one was the platform’s biggest ever UK launch. The show later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme. “I don’t want to overplay the jump scares,” says Carr – who first persuaded the channel to develop a UK version of what was originally a Japanese hit. “There’s nothing that would trouble anyone. It’s not that kind of show. It’s just fun. It’s ‘event TV’ – especially when it’s tied around something like Halloween – that’s great for bringing people together.”

And for bringing comedians together too – the more so now LOL has joined Taskmaster as the shop window par excellence for standups making the leap from fringe to mainstream. Alongside national-treasure veterans (Bob Mortimer in series one; Mel Giedroyc in series two), Last One Laughing reserves places for up-and-coming acts – see recent Edinburgh comedy award winner Harriet Dyer here. Getting involved, she says, was “a whirlwind, to be honest. But it was a dream come true.” All the participating comics agree, mind you, that you can’t treat LOL like a career opportunity. “You can’t play it like that,” says Tom Allen. “You have to engulf yourself in the moment. And that reveals people’s true character. There’s something very vulnerable about laughing. We feel very open when we do it.”

Few comics are more oversharingly their own self than Lou Sanders, a late casualty (red-carded by Carr in episode six) in series one, now returning for series 2.5. There’s a strict embargo on spoilers today, but when I ask Sanders if previous experience gave her an advantage in the Halloween outing, her response does not suggest a triumphant comeback. “I thought I would be better,” she says. “But I was immediately on the back foot. And Reece got into my head early on.” Then there’s the knowledge that millions are watching. On series one, “Joe Wilkinson said to me ‘no one’s going to watch this,’ and I believed him. And then it did well. This time, you know there’s going to be eyes on it.”

Sanders has been charged with giving me a tour of the LOL house, a bar cum living room cum art deco theatre, like a prefab 1920s ocean liner constructed in a ginormous Elstree hangar. Here is the fruit machine that’s used to prompt new challenges. There the stage on which contestants perform their ‘joker’ party pieces – around which more strictures circulate than you’d expect. (“I thought it would be funny to have a fire on my head,” says Harriet Dyer. “But I was told: no fire. Then I wanted long arms, but I wasn’t allowed them … ”) There are also creepy dolls, just for Halloween. Does it get claustrophobic in here, I ask Sanders? “I wasn’t in here long enough to know” comes her doleful reply.

But if Sanders’ tactics proved inadequate, others enter Last One Laughing with sophisticated strategies all mapped out. “My tactic was to channel Dame Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey,” says Tom Allen. “Very aloof, very lofty. So I channelled everything through my eyebrows, rather than a lot of people, who try not to laugh by biting the inside of their mouth.” Wang had a more attacking approach. “My mantra was: a good defence is a good offence. Get on the front foot, try to get to people. Focus on those you know at first, because you know what makes them tick. And while doing that, watch the people you don’t know, to see what makes them laugh.”

Dyer entered the house with an idea of what not to do. “I think Sam Campbell said on series two that he thought about, like, kids dying to stop himself laughing. So I thought: should I focus on the worst thing that’s ever happened to me? But I’m not sure watching someone be traumatised with what life’s thrown at them makes for very good telly.” Campbell is the maverick Aussie comic who tested the show’s conceit to breaking point last time around, by staying po-faced from start to finish. He eventually lost in a tie-break to David Mitchell. “We nearly broke David,” says Jimmy Carr. “At the end he was going, ‘I don’t think I’ll ever laugh again. I’ve lost that part of myself for ever’.”

Series two’s other breaking point was reached when – great controversy, this – the comic Amy Gledhill was red-carded by Carr for smiling rather than laughing. My own household can’t have been alone in its outrage at this disregard for the show’s core conceit. But Carr is unrepentant. “I mean, we’d got to that stage of the day,” he says: something had to give. “And it’s that water cooler thing: as long as people are arguing about it and having fun, so much the better.”

To Carr, the show is as much sports as entertainment: the key, he thinks, to its success. “There’s a narrative to sports, whereby you’ve got to watch to the end because you don’t know what’s going to happen. And that’s the same thing with this show: it’s competitive, and you want to know who’s going to win.” “And each episode ends on a really effective cliffhanger,” adds Phil Wang, “which is quite hard to achieve with comedy.”

The other clincher, for Carr and the comics, is how rigorously LOL is produced. Says Carr, “the other countries don’t do the set pieces we do”: the guest appearances, the challenges, the props and tricks contestants can bring to the table – much to Lou Sanders’ dismay. “Reece Shearsmith is Mr Halloween, isn’t he? He’s got all that stuff at home! It’s not fair. I haven’t got a severed hand at home, have I?”

According to Wang, “shows that prepare more than they need always prosper. And this show definitely prepares more than it needs.” Every contestant has a camera trained on them throughout, and a dedicated “spotter” hanging on their every smirk. “I presented it in the room yesterday for nine hours,” says Carr. “But I haven’t seen it all yet. When you get in the edit, there’s a whole other show there. There’s all the conversations people have on the screens I’m not watching. I remember on series two discovering all these incredible moments with Diane Morgan we just didn’t know were there.”

The lineup has already been announced for LOL series three, which broadcasts next year. Harry Hill, Katherine Ryan and Lee Mack all feature. What advice – or warnings – would the Halloween participants impart? “You end up in there for so long,” says Wang – lucky for some! – “that your mood goes from giddy and excited to paranoid and nervous. I was doing a lot of pinching, a lot of breathing, a lot of meditation and mindfulness.” It was, says Tom Allen, “an intense experience, trying to withhold two emotions and not let them out of the bag. It’s exhausting.”

But it’s all in the service, says Allen, of something much needed in our not-always-joyful times. “The series speaks to a childlike sense of play, one that reminds us of being in assembly or in class at school and not being allowed to laugh. There’s nothing more exquisite than that burning desire to laugh while having to keep a lid on it, the steam cooker pressure that brings. Last One Laughing returns us to that youthful joy. I think it’s something people really crave.”

Last One Laughing: Halloween is on Prime Video from Friday.

Entertainment.title: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top
Entertainment.text:
Leaving the important stuff to chance isn’t Shygirl’s style. First aid kit, wind-up radio, batteries: earlier this morning, the singer filled her online shopping basket in preparation for impending disaster. She had read a news article advising households to put together an emergency kit. “I’m that kind of person,” she says, grinning. She woke her boyfriend, who was asleep in bed next to her. “I was like: babe, we’re sorted! I’ve got the water purifying tablets, everything!”

It’s a sticky September afternoon in east London, and the singer, whose real name is Blane Muise, introduces herself as “Shy” and slides into the booth opposite me at an Italian trattoria. She first burst on to the club scene with the naughty, pulsating Want More in 2016, and in the decade since, the singer, rapper and DJ has applied the same rigour to her career as she has to her emergency prepping, going from cult underground artist to rising pop star, opening arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx, winning a Mobo award in 2024, and appearing in Madonna’s recent Confessions II – The Film, in which she shared a toilet stall with Arca and Richard E Grant.

She has also grafted hard at falling in love and entering a long-term relationship, which is the subject of her forthcoming second album, Swallow!. An epic, soaring rock record, with more than a touch of William Orbit-era Madonna, it is an ode to intimacy, vulnerability and mutual devotion. Love, she says, is “scary, exciting and big”. The 33-year-old’s particular mix of hard and soft, of brash swagger, blunt humour and slippery feminine desire has found an exhilarating new form of expression.

In December 2022, Shygirl was preparing to go on tour. Her debut album Nymph had received rave reviews and she was finally earning enough money from music to rent her own place. “I felt good about the reception, but there’s always that anticlimactic feeling when you get what you wanted. You’re like: OK, now I have it. Now what?” she says, tossing her tangerine corkscrew curls. “Then I met George.”

Go on, I say, tell me the story. “It was on Raya,” she says conspiratorially. She was hungover from a night out while browsing the members-only dating app. When they matched, she asked him to send a voice note: “I don’t like meeting up with people unless I can hear what they sound like and their cadence.” Satisfied, she invited him over to watch one of her favourite films, Alien. “Then we got Thai takeout and hooked up,” she says matter-of-factly.

She was leaving for Australia later that week, but they kept talking for almost two months. When she decided to extend her trip and add a visit to Japan, “I was like: fuck it. Do you wanna come to Tokyo?” She flew him out – “in economy”, she says, laughing – and she and actor George Smale have been together ever since. “We had 10 days there and one other date in London when I got back before saying, ‘I love you.’” By the summer, they’d moved in together. Unlike previous relationships, she says, “I didn’t feel like I was all of a sudden so enamoured with someone that I didn’t know where my footing was.”

That contentment and calm was a source of inspiration. “When I made Lucky, I sat in the room with the mic. I didn’t write anything down, I just said how I felt,” she says of the album’s lead single. “It’s me saying: I am an active participant because of the choices that brought me here.” Like many of the tracks on Swallow!, Lucky[Hymn] is an indie song. “It had more of a classic tone to it because I felt like I was in a classic part of my life,” she says.

With its dreamy, moody guitars and anthemic, crashing drums, Swallow! is a different sound for an artist whose previous records have flirted with hyperpop, UK garage and electronica. As a millennial, Shygirl came of age when guitar-driven pop music was dominating the charts. “It was very prevalent in all the pop I grew up listening to: Keane, Madonna, random shit like the Rasmus,” she says. In the 2010s, when she was a teenager, musical discovery was serendipitous: “We had HMV, where you could just walk in and put the headphones on.” Her curiosity, she says, was encouraged by her parents. “I’m not from a family where they would just give you answers.”

Shygirl is the eldest of three children born to young parents in south-east London, and spent her early years bouncing between Downham, Catford and Lee Green. “My life has shown me that you are never entitled to anything,” she says. “You can be deserving but not receive.” When has she felt like that? “I grew up with that experience. My parents worked really hard. They didn’t have everything.”

Her dad, who is of Grenadian origin, worked for the UK government’s Welsh office and later as a club promoter in Notting Hill. She didn’t see him much when he was working nights. Meanwhile, “my mum used to work as a cleaner, a toilet attendant, a receptionist, a dinner lady,” she says. “She’s always had a job.” So has Shygirl, who as a teenager worked at a restaurant her mum managed.

Her parents are no longer together, though she is quick to clarify that hers was a happy childhood. “I wanted for nothing,” she says. “But I’m of the mindset that if you want something, you have to go get it. I’m only the one to blame if I don’t.” That determination runs through new songs such as Live the Life You Like, a stomping, Prodigy-esque anthem. “And then I’m pushing / It’s not enough,” she purrs.

In Amsterdam, in 2018, she booked her first show before her debut EP, Cruel Practice, had even been released. “I was like: I don’t even have any music out and someone’s taken a chance on me,” she remembers. Soon afterwards she handed in her notice as a booker at a modelling agency. “I’m about to quit a day job that had holiday pay, sick pay, and I’m gonna go be a musician? But because I used to do contracts with the model agency, I knew how to push a rate up.” She negotiated requests from brands who wanted to use her music in their adverts, until one came in from Rihanna, for Fenty Beauty, and she got overexcited – “not as sharky as I usually am” with making the deal. She got a manager, the money came in and Shygirl paid off her credit card. She likens herself to a gambler: “My money was up from being, like, two grand in debt. I’d owed my housemate money for rent.”

She signed a record deal in 2020; this year, she bought a house. She hadn’t even entertained owning one, “because I was so busy thinking I need to pay my rent and bills. My dad still doesn’t own a house. My mum just got one.” Her drive to make music, she says, “has always been to make my life better than my origins, and to prove to my family that their sacrifice is worth something”. But “living an experience they have never lived” has been accompanied by a dose of “mad guilt”.

She played New York’s Madison Square Garden with Charli xcx and Troye Sivan as 2024’s Brat summer raged on into Brat autumn. Seeing how Charli, a peer and friend, was able to maintain her sense of self even as everything became “as big and stressful as it gets” made pop domination feel more achievable. Although, “we definitely have different intentions for our day to day”. Charli, she stresses, works incredibly hard. “I work hard, but I really prioritise chilling,” she laughs.

Spending an afternoon hanging out with Shygirl, as she radiates self-possession, grace and plenty of gossipy wisdom, one gets the sense that she is something of a girl’s girl. “All of us are trying to open doors for each other – all the female artists that I’ve worked with.” Being a woman, she says, is her biggest barrier as an artist. “In my experience, that is the most prevalent block at the moment.” She gives the example of Beyoncé’s Grammy win for best country album with Cowboy Carter, which prompted the Recording Academy to create two separate categories for best country album: traditional and contemporary. “The rules shift, and the doors’ locations change,” she says.

Realising there might be a ceiling for her ambition, one imposed on her by others, has meant she is now “only interested in working with people who want different-ness. Who are not comfortable with the status quo, because I can’t relate to that. It’s not an experience I’ve had in any avenue of my life.” And, she adds, “it’s usually men” upholding that status quo. “Not to be a man hater: I love my boyfriend!”

Shygirl and Smale have been collaborating creatively, too. He provided background vocals on album opener Alyse and they have worked together on the interconnected videos for the new album, which she co-directed and which form an elliptical thriller narrative based around a kidnapping. “You’re dropped into a situation the same as The Bourne Ultimatum or Tell No One. You may have been an ordinary person; you’re now in extraordinary circumstances: what do you do?” she says. Her character ends up tied to a chair. She seldom even thinks of not acting in any situation, she says, so it was a challenge to play someone barely able to move.

But her character screams, shouts, cries and thrashes as she’s held captive, giving Shygirl an outlet for emotions she didn’t realise she needed to express. “I never raise my voice,” she says. “To shout at someone who has made you angry? To show that you’re affected by them in that way? I would never do that.” An eldest daughter, she describes herself as a protector who feels responsible for everyone else in her life. “I feel like every child gets to a point where they see their parents as human beings, not just as their caregivers. That happened for me when I was very young.” How young? “Ten, 12.” It meant she never had idols. “I don’t really look up to anyone in that way,” she says. “I see everyone with faults.”

In the video’s final shot, Shygirl looks directly into the lens, “accepting that this is a contrived environment”. She wanted to break the fourth wall, even if that movie trope is a bit of a cliche: “Sometimes cliches are cliches for a reason, you know?”

Of course, falling in love is the biggest cliche of all, I add. “Exactly!” Once you’ve said “I love you” a million times to your partner, she says, “you’re looking for other ways to express it”. Her smile is beatific thinking about it all. Playing the new album to her boyfriend made her cry; the delicate, intensely vulnerable ballad Real allowed her “to revisit the memory of when we were in Japan, and recognise that now as falling in love”. It has an incredulous, awestruck quality, as though she can’t believe her own good fortune. “We’re always choosing each other,” she says. “I’m always choosing what’s happening in my life.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he is "only standing up for Ukraine's interests" after scathing criticism from Donald Trump, who said Kyiv's new wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries was a "disgrace".

The US president, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import diesel, also said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".

Zelensky, who has been angered by the diesel deal, said he could not accept it, because a gas agreement could come next. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" he said at an EU summit in Brussels.

Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated over the diesel deal and curbs on Ukraine's battlefield satellite network.

Zelensky's trip to Brussels, following a visit to London, has come at the end of a bruising week. As he arrived at the summit on Friday, where EU leaders rallied around him in support, Zelensky said it was good to be back among allies. "Leaders, real leaders," he said, in a possible slight to the US president.

At the summit, funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the agenda.

The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.

Zelensky said that while Ukraine could produce up to three times more drones, it "simply [doesn't] have enough money for that".

A fundamental problem for Kyiv - which cannot be easily fixed - is the chronic lack of US-made Patriot missiles to defend its towns and cities.

Zelensky said he believed Europe did possess all the interceptors his country would need this winter but described them as being scooped up in a piecemeal fashion.

Zelensky also addressed Ukraine's frayed relationship with the US, saying there are "many people with good hearts in America" who want "to be allies, not to divide or humiliate Europe".

Trump has heavily criticised Zelensky for resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries earlier this week, because it could impact Moscow's ability to complete its part of the diesel deal, which will see 300,000 tonnes of diesel sent to "the American and global marketplace".

As both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking each other's energy infrastructure, Trump suddenly announced a ceasefire on the facilities last week.

Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same, but Moscow said it had never agreed to the deal and continued its attacks. After three days, Kyiv resumed its strikes.

Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine.

The US president said he was "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he was "not a good guy for us to deal with".

"He doesn't want to settle," Trump said. "He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't."

"As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled."

When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said of Zelensky: "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit."

Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russia's oil facilities, because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US has made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices.

Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump's standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections.

At a news conference after the EU summit, Zelensky was asked if he felt that Trump was using him as a scapegoat for his own political problems. After a pause, the president broke into a grin, prompting laughter from the journalists in the room.

"This is my answer," he said.

The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and on Friday said it would "put more money straight into Putin's pocket to fund this war".

His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.

During the slowdown on Tuesday night, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning.

On Friday, Zelensky called the slowdown a "very dangerous and unpleasant surprise", adding that Starlink speeds were still not fully restored.

The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence-sharing - crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tiger attack medical records may have been breached
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Trust, a spokesperson has said.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.

In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.

They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.

"We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.

"The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals.

"We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.

The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.

"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.

Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.

"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.

Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."

But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.

There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."

In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.

As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.

Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.

The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.

Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.

What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' Johannes Natland detained for UK murder plot
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."

Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.

When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed.

"There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan.

"We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."

Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.

Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school.

He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".

He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.

Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".

The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."

Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.

He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.

Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.

He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.

The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets.

"You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."

From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room.

Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.

The Norwegian lawyers acting for the 19-year-old said they would work to have him transferred to Norway to serve his sentence.

"Twenty years is a very severe sentence for a boy who was 18 when he was arrested," they said in a statement.

"The other young people convicted in the related proceedings in Norway mainly received youth sentences or community sentences.

"We will take the time to consider the sentence carefully, together with him, his family and his British legal team."

Counter Terrorism Policing said it continued to investigate those suspected of helping Natland obtain firearms and a stolen car.

In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and was later released under investigation.

Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods, specifically a car.

They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital,in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.

Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.

On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.

His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".

The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.

"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.

Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.

The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.

"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.

His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.

"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said.

The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.

She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused".

The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet.

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

The woman gave evidence on Friday from behind a screen at Southwark Crown Court in London, on the third day of Brand's trial.

She told the jury the alleged incident at MTV lasted for about 20 seconds, adding: "It was a very short exchange."

Asked how she felt after the alleged attack by Brand, the woman said: "Bewildered, confused, 'what the hell happened there?'"

She said Brand went from someone who was "affable" to a "wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet".

"I was confused that that actually just happened - anyone would be," she said.

The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

The woman was speaking after a former flatmate of Brand's, Andrew Dobson, earlier told the jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer.

Dobson gave evidence after another woman told the court on Thursday that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999.

She said she had met Brand, before he was famous, while she was attending the Labour Party conference.

Dobson told the court on Friday he attended the Bournemouth conference and had written music for a fringe event that Brand was part of.

Karmy-Jones asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous.

Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical".

"I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term."

Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand.

He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand.

The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members.

The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard.

Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried".

The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?"

Dobson replied: "I can't recall anything specific that was said. I only remember the atmosphere and panicked, urgent. Feeling tense and confusing."

He went on to tell the jury there had been an "abrupt change of atmosphere" from what had been a "fun week" to an "abrupt change of tone".

Under cross-examination by Brand's barrister, it was put to Dobson that in his witness statement he said that Brand was one of few men he knew that women would swoon over.

Dobson replied: "He was certainly charismatic".

Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

However, he described Scotland as the most devolved nation in the UK but "one of the most centralised in Europe".

"During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities," he said.

"Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.

"This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people."

The Scottish government set out plans for a radical rethink of the country's regional authorities last month.

A new two-tiered system would see the 32 local authorities replaced with six new regional authorities.

They would have power over major issues such as economic growth and education.

Below that, between 120 and 160 community authorities would govern more local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.

It would be the most significant change to Scotland's regional makeup since the current system was introduced by the UK government in 1996.

Burnham acknowledged that the Scottish government was working on local government reform, but said this had to "move faster".

It is not clear exactly what powers might be exercised at regional level other than employment support.

Burnham appears to expect the Scottish government to devolve some of its own powers to regional authorities.

But he made clear that he will not impose a model of regional devolution like the metropolitan mayors that already operate in England.

Instead he wants to try and agree a way forward with further discussions when the prime minister sits down with all the devolved first ministers at the end of this month.

Burnham also called for an end to "tribal politics" between the Scottish and UK governments.

He said he and Swinney "agreed on some things" but "didn't have to agree on everything".

Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday.

He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs that a border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Ireland if there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.

But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".

Asked whether devolving power more locally in Scotland would make independence more or less likely, the prime minister said: "I don't want to be the last PM of the UK.

"I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.

"In my view, people in Scotland are suffering from the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else, and I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people right now."

He added: "Too much time is wasted on those dramas, it consumes too much energy."

Stephen Flynn - who was the SNP's leader at Westminster before becoming the Transport Secretary at Holyrood - said the Scottish government would welcome the opportunity to be handed more power over the country's economic prospects.

He said: "Interestingly the first minister sent a letter to the prime minister on Monday where he outlined a number of points he would like to see engagement on.

"This was number seven on that list, so we will of course engage with the prime minister fully in respect of his announcement today."

Before Burnham's speech, First Minister John Swinney said he was interested in "working constructively" with Westminster, adding he was "all for the Scottish Parliament having as many powers" as possible.

UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham should be focusing on creating new opportunities in the energy sector.

She said: "This regional devolution plan is more jobs for the boys. What Andy Burnham should be doing is granting new oil and gas licences in the north sea."

"Devolution is a process, not a solution."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Action needed to save water, minister tells MPs
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The government has warned action is needed to prevent water shortages becoming "the norm" after severe drought was declared across parts of southern England.

Water and flooding minister Emma Hardy told MPs current drought conditions were "something we have not experienced for decades" and urged people to "think about ways to use water wisely over the coming weeks".

Severe drought was declared across parts of southern England on Thursday after months of low rainfall, with around 50 million people now impacted.

Parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex are all affected by the move announced by the Environment Agency.

The government said supplies would not be interrupted but declaring severe drought would ensure "proactive steps are taken to safeguard water before any disruption occurs".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Hardy said the measures were down to "exceptionally low rainfall" and depleted reservoir levels.

The minister noted Yorkshire also moved into drought status last week.

"That means over 80% of England is now in drought, affecting around 50 million people," she said.

"The South East and South West, in particular, have experienced their driest April to September in over a century.

"While the record-breaking heat and lack of rainfall have put our water resources under immense pressure this year, we must take action now to prevent this situation becoming the norm."

Robbie Moore, shadow minister for environment, food and rural affairs, accused the government of being "slow to react" to the conditions.

"This is the third drought in five years, it should not have caught the government off guard," he told MPs.

Hardy insisted "we know that this the new normal when it comes to our weather", adding: "This is exactly why we are preparing for it."

The Environment Agency was also expected to increase compliance checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources to ensure they only take permitted quantities.

It said "small changes" including taking shorter showers, fixing leaks and turning off taps while brushing teeth could "make a real difference".

"These aren't token gestures," the agency said.

"They cut the amount of water we need to take from rivers and groundwater, protecting supplies for people and leaving more for wildlife, wetlands and the natural systems we all depend on."

The Environment Agency said further dry weather was expected for the rest of October: "The usual seasonal rainfall has yet to arrive, and 82% of England remains in drought."

In some areas, 120% of the expected rainfall was needed for the next six months or "drought conditions will continue and could worsen", it said.

Severe drought is the most serious level, and was declared "when evidence shows drought is causing, or will soon cause, serious harm, and that emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Beth Dobbin: British Olympic sprinter in bed for 22 hours a day after ME diagnosis
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.

"I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says.

"But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out."

She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom.

Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.

A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.

This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions.

"It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything.

"I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise."

For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests.

She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself.

British Athletics doctors ran tests that gave no answers, so she carried on, assuming it was lingering glandular fever that would eventually pass.

She qualified for that year's World Championships, Commonwealth Games and European Championships in what was an unusually condensed season owing to the backlog from the pandemic.

Her health progressively deteriorated. At the Worlds, she struggled with a painful throat and was waking at unusual times in the night. At the Commonwealths, she was dizzy while running and her body was more sore than normal.

At the Europeans, she false-started after losing all feeling in her legs while in the blocks. She spoke of her "year of hell" in an emotional interview with BBC Sport after that race.

"When the Europeans had finished, I had this huge rest and the symptoms were just piling on. Things were getting worse and worse," Dobbin says. "I was struggling to stand up, I was sleeping loads, in bed all the time.

"After six weeks, I went back to training. I managed three weeks.

"[Doctors] were just really shocked that I still wasn't doing well and I'd had these viruses months ago.

"I think I saw four or five different specialists because the symptoms that I was having, they were across multiple [body] systems. All the specialists said 'this is ME' and we don't want it to be that because there's nothing out there for it."

ME has no known cure or specific treatment, with patients often relying on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.

The condition is also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), a label Dobbin strongly rejects. As a former athlete who balanced working eight-hour shifts with training before turning professional, she says she has "known fatigue my whole life" and believes the term fails to capture the severity of the illness.

"I wish it was just fatigue, that would be a walk in the park," she says. "It's so much more than that. If I thought of fatigue in my top 20 symptoms it might just make the cut."

Instead, she says, it feels like her entire body "is shutting down; it feels like you are a few days from death".

More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.

Despite the length of time she spends in bed, Dobbin often feels too unwell to sleep and requires medication to help her do so.

"Even things like sitting up for a prolonged period of time can take it out of me so I prefer to be just propped up in bed, and that doesn't mean I feel fine. It doesn't get rid of my symptoms, but it makes them less hellish."

For Dobbin's parents and sister Faye, who sit close by to her in support during the interview at the family home in Doncaster, the impact is clear.

"I'm just so desperate to help her but I can't because there is nothing. I'd take her anywhere, I'd take her to America if I had to, but there's nothing," says her father Jim, a former footballer who played for Barnsley, Grimsby and Doncaster Rovers.

Mum Jean adds: "You wake up every day and just feel sad. She should be building her life, living her best life.

"Every day you worry about how she's going to be that day. It's a worry about what our future life's going to be like, who's going look after her if we can't look after her.

"There is nothing out there. There is nowhere to go. You go to the GP and there's nowhere for them to send you to. It's really at the back of the queue as far as research, knowledge, expertise, funding."

There are limited specialist services for ME within the NHS and Dobbin says she has found herself educating the GPs she spoke to about the condition.

She had to wait 22 months before she got a face-to-face appointment with a private specialist she sourced herself after her British Athletics funding ended.

On Sunday, Dobbin's younger sister Faye will run the Yorkshire Marathon to raise money for ME Research UK.

"You just feel so helpless and we've been saying this for years now, what can we do?" Faye says.

"It feels like [the marathon] is all I can do other than supporting her emotionally.

"It does feel quite like grief in a way. I'm always worried about Beth. She's always on my mind. I'm worried about what kind of day she is having. What if she never improves? What if she gets worse? What if she gets another virus?"

Asked about her future, Dobbin is straight to the point: "It's very bleak, unfortunately.

"The only positive thing really to say is that Covid happened six years ago now and it's like the whole medical community has woken up."

Since the Covid pandemic and the emergence of long Covid, for which there is a significant overlap in symptoms with ME, there has been a surge in attention and increase in research funding for the condition.

She added: "There will be something, I hope, in the future.

"I said I wanted to speak about it. It's not necessarily that I want to discuss it [but] it's raising that awareness. And unfortunately, athletes are believed a lot more than the average person.

"A lot of people that have this illness that I've spoken to have said to me 'I don't get believed, people think I'm lazy'. I've never experienced one person that doesn't believe me and that's because, why would an athlete just suddenly stop after 20 years?

"I've got a slight platform. If this happened to most people they wouldn't be able to speak about it, so I do feel like I've got a bit of a duty to do that."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.

Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".

The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.

The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.

Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.

Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
